For the Petitioner: Mr. N.K. Thakur, Senior Advocate with Mr. Divya
 Raj Singh, Advocate.

For the Respondents: Mr. Rajan Kahol, Mr. Vishal Panwar and Mr. B.C.
 Verma, Additional Advocates General with Mr. Ravi  Chauhan, Deputy Advocates General.

Bail petitioner namely Davinder Singh, who is behind the bars since 12.1.2024, has approached this court in the instant proceedings filed under Section 439 Cr.PC, for grant of regular bail, in case FIR No. 3/24 dated 12.1.2024, registered at Women Police Station Una, District Una, Himachal Pradesh,
under Sections 376, 506, 341 and 120B of IPC.
2.

sentences.text:
In terms of order dated 15.5.2024, respondent-State has filed the status report and pursuant to notices issued in the instant proceedings, Mr. Ashwani Kaundal Advocate, has put in appearance on .
behalf of the Victim.

3. Close scrutiny of status report as well as other material made available to this Court reveals that on 12.1.2024, victim-prosecutrix (name withheld), lodged a complaint that her marriage was solemnized in May, 2023, with person namely Amit Kumar, out of their wedlock, one male child was born in December, 2023.
She alleged that the bail petitioner is married with her cousin and he had been visiting her house since January, 2023.
She alleged that in January, 2023, bail petitioner visited her house and expressed his intention to maintain physical relations with her but she refused.

She alleged that in January 2023, at 5:00am,
when she had gone for jogging and had reached near Crematorium, bail petitioner was standing there.
She alleged that bail petitioner obstructed her path and forcibly took her to a nearby hut/shack and committed forcible sexual intercourse with her.
She alleged that since bail petitioner extended threats, she did not disclose such fact to anybody.
She alleged that again, in the month of March, 2023, she was again subjected to sexual intercourse in the presence of a person namely Harish alias Happy.
She alleged that though above named Happy also pressurized her to maintain physical relations with him, but she refused.
She alleged that on 28.3.2023, again bail petitioner called her near Shamshan Ghat and sexually assaulted her against her wishes.

. 
She alleged that since bail petitioner threatened that he would make the video viral, she was unable to disclose afore facts to anybody.
She alleged that after some time, she came to know about the pregnancy from the bail petitioner and on 8.12.2023, she delivered a child, which belongs to the petitioner.
She alleged that on account of pregnancy from the bail petitioner, her husband as well as other members of his family have disowned her.
In the aforesaid background, FIR, as detailed herein above, came to be lodged against the bail petitioner on 12.1.2024 and since then, he is behind the bars.

Since challan stands filed in the competent court of law and nothing remains to be recovered from the bail petitioner, he has approached this Court in the instant proceedings, praying therein for grant of regular bail.

4. Mr. Vishal Panwar, learned Additional Advocate General, while acknowledging factum with regard to filing of the challan in the competent court of law, states that though nothing remains to _____________________________________________________________________ vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150708374/
2 be recovered from the bail petitioner, but keeping in view the gravity of offence alleged to have been committed by him, he does not deserves any leniency.

Mr. Panwar, submits that though at the time of the alleged incident, victim-prosecutrix was major, but since she was under constant threat from the bail petitioner, she was unable to report the matter to the police well within .
time and as such, delay, if any in lodging FIR may not be a ground for the petitioner to claim bail.

While referring to the medical record adduced on record, Mr. Panwar, contends that child delivered by victim-prosecutrix on 8.12.2023, is of the bail petitioner as has been opined by the FSL while rendering opinion on the basis of DNA Test.

5. Mr. Ashwani Kaundal, Advocate, appearing on behalf of the Victim, while opposing prayer made by the petitioner for grant of bail, contends that repeatedly, victim-prosecutrix was subjected to forcible sexual intercourse by the petitioner against her wishes.

He submits that there is ample evidence collected on record by the prosecution suggestive of the fact that victim prosecutrix was subjected to sexual intercourse under threat that in case she reveals such fact to anybody, video allegedly made of the incident shall be made viral.

Mr. Kaundal, further submits that though victim-prosecutrix was major at the time of the incident, but once there is overwhelming evidence suggestive of the fact that bail petitioner alongwith other co-accused Harish had been extending threats, it would be too premature to conclude that there was consent, if any, on the part of the victim-prosecutrix.

Lastly, Mr. Kaundal, submits that even after lodging of FIR, as detailed herein abvoe, victim is being threatened by his family members as well as co-accused Harish, who already stands enlarged on .
bail.
6. Having heard learned counsel for the parties and perused the material available on record, this Court finds that at the time of the alleged incident, victim-prosecutrix was major.
As per own statement of victim- prosecutrix, she had prior acquaintance with the bail petitioner, who had been visiting her house since January, 2023.

No doubt, bail petitioner subsequently, solemnized marriage with cousin of the victim-prosecutrix, but as per own statement of victim-prosecutrix, she was subjected to forcible sexual intercourse in January, 2023, by the bail petitioner.

There is nothing on record suggestive of the fact that in January, 2023, victim- prosecutrix made an attempt to lodge complaint against the conduct of the bail petitioner either to the family members or to the police, rather, she repeatedly succumbed to the pressure of the bail petitioner, who allegedly after January, 2023, subjected her to forcible sexual intercourse on three occasions.

Though it has been claimed by victim-prosecutrix that she never wanted to spoil the family of the cousin, but it is not understood that once she was being repeatedly sexually assaulted that too by her brother in law, where was the occasion for her to keep mum.

Moreover, this Court finds that repeatedly, victim-prosecutrix went to the place chosen by the .
bail petitioner i.e. Shamshan Ghat.
_____________________________________________________________________ vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150708374/
3 7.
Interestingly, two incidents of sexual assault allegedly happened at 5:00am that too near Shamshan Ghat.

As per statement of the victim-prosecutrix, on one occasion, she was subjected to forcible sexual intercourse by the petitioner in the presence of the co-accused Harish alias Happy,
who though has been named in the FIR, but at present stands enlarged on bail.

It clearly emerges from the record that factum with regard to relationship inter-se bail petitioner and victim-prosecutrix came to the fore in December 2023, when victim-prosecutrix delivered a child,
who has been now opined by the medical authorities to be child of the bail petitioner.

No doubt,
medical evidence adduced on record clearly establishes that bail petitioner is the biological father of the child delivered by the victim-prosecutrix in the month of December, 2023, but such fact may not be sufficient to conclude guilt, if any, of the petitioner for his having committed offence punishable under Section 376 of the IPC, especially when own conduct of the victim-prosecutrix, which is apparent from the record, suggests something else.

8. Though it has been claimed by the victim-prosecutrix that she subjected herself to the desires of the petitioner on account of repeated threats, but having taken note of the fact that victim-prosecutrix at the .
time of the alleged incident was major, coupled with the fact that bail petitioner was his brother in law, this Court finds it difficult to agree with Mr. Ashwani Kaundal, learned counsel appearing for the Victim that on account of constant threat, victim-prosecutrix was unable to report the matter to the police or family.

9. Though aforesaid aspects of the matter are to be decided by the court below in the totality of evidence collected on record by the prosecution, but having noticed conduct of the victim-prosecutrix, which certainly indicates towards consent of the victim-prosecutrix, this Court sees no reason to let the bail petitioners incarcerate in jail for an indefinite period during trial,
especially when nothing remains to be recovered from them.
10. Hon'ble Apex Court as well as this Court in catena of cases have repeatedly held that one is deemed to be innocent till the time guilt, if any, of his/her is not proved in accordance with law.

Since factum of threatening caution, if any, exercised by the petitioner is yet to be proved by the prosecution, by leading cogent and convincing evidence, this Court sees no reason to curtail the freedom of the bail petitioner indefinitely during trial.

Apprehension expressed by the learned Additional Advocate General as well as Mr. Ashwani Kundal, Advocate that in the event of .
petitioner's being enlarged on bail, he may flee from justice, can be best met by putting the bail petitioners to stringent conditions as has been fairly stated by the learned counsel for the petitioner.
11.

Needless to say, object of the bail is to secure the attendance of the accused in the trial and the proper test to be applied in the solution of the question whether bail should be granted or refused is whether it is probable that the party will appear to take his trial.
Otherwise, bail is not to be withheld as a punishment.
Otherwise also, normal rule is of bail and not jail.

Court has to keep in mind nature of accusations, nature of evidence in support thereof, severity of the punishment which conviction will entail, character of the accused, circumstances which are peculiar to the accused _____________________________________________________________________ vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150708374/
4 involved in that crime.
12. The Hon'ble Apex Court in Sanjay Chandra versus Central Bureau of Investigation (2012)1 Supreme Court Cases 49; held as under:-

entities.text: Sanjay Chandra versus Central Bureau of Investigation (2012)1 Supreme Court Cases 49
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: " The object of bail is to secure the appearance of the accused person at his trial by reasonable amount of bail.
The object of bail is neither punitive nor preventative.
Deprivation of liberty must be considered a punishment, unless it can be required to ensure that an accused person will stand his trial when called upon.

The Courts owe more than verbal respect to the principle that punishment begins after conviction,
and that every man is deemed to be innocent until duly tried and duly found guilty.
Detention in custody pending completion of trial could be a cause of great hardship.

From time to time, necessity demands that some unconvicted persons should be held in custody pending trial to secure their attendance at the trial but in such cases,
"necessity" is the operative test.

In India , it would be quite contrary to the concept of personal liberty enshrined in the .
Constitution that any person should be punished in respect of any matter, upon which, he has not been convicted or that in any circumstances, he should be deprived of his liberty upon only the belief that he will tamper with the witnesses if left at liberty, save in the most extraordinary circumstances.

Apart from the question of prevention being the object of refusal of bail, one must not lose sight of the fact that any imprisonment before conviction has a substantial punitive content and it would be improper for any court to refuse bail as a mark of disapproval of former conduct whether the accused has been convicted for it or not or to refuse bail to an unconvicted person for the propose of giving him a taste of imprisonment as a lesson."

13. In Manoranjana Sinh Alias Gupta versus CBI 2017 (5) SCC 218, The Hon'ble Apex Court has held as under:-
" This Court in Sanjay Chandra v. CBI, also involving an economic offence of formidable magnitude, while dealing with the issue of grant of bail, had observed that deprivation of liberty must be considered a punishment unless it is required to ensure that an accused person would stand his trial when called upon and that the courts owe more than verbal respect to the principle that punishment begins after conviction and that every man is deemed to be innocent until duly tried and found guilty.

entities.text: Manoranjana Sinh Alias Gupta versus CBI 2017 (5) SCC 218
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: It was underlined that the object of bail is neither punitive or preventive.

This Court sounded a caveat that any imprisonment before conviction has a substantial punitive content and it would be improper for any court to refuse bail as a mark of disapproval of a conduct whether an accused has been convicted for it or not or to refuse bail to an unconvicted person for the purpose of giving him to taste of imprisonment as a lesson.

It was enunciated that since the jurisdiction to grant bail to an accused pending trial or in appeal against conviction is discretionary in nature,
_____________________________________________________________________ vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150708374/
5
it has to be exercised with care ad caution by balancing the valuable right of liberty of an individual and the interest of the society in general.

It was elucidated that the seriousness of the charge, is no doubt one of the relevant considerations while examining the application of bail but it was not only the test or the factor and the grant or denial of such privilege, is regulated to a large extent by the facts and circumstances of each particular case.
That detention in custody of under trial prisoners for an indefinite period would amount to violation of Article 21 of the Constitution was highlighted."

14. Hon'ble Apex Court in Criminal Appeal No. 227/2018, Dataram Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr., decided on 6.2.2018, has categorically held that a fundamental postulate of criminal .
jurisprudence is the presumption of innocence, meaning thereby that a person is believed to be innocent until found guilty.

entities.text: Dataram Singh vs. State of Uttar Pradesh & Anr
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: Hon'ble Apex Court further held that while considering prayer for grant of bail, it is important to ascertain whether the accused was participating in the investigations to the satisfaction of the investigating officer and was not absconding or not appearing when required by the investigating officer.

Hon'ble Apex Court further held that if an accused is not hiding from the investigating officer or is hiding due to some genuine and expressed fear of being victimized, it would be a factor that a judge would need to consider in an appropriate case.

The relevant paras of the aforesaid judgment are reproduced as under:
"2. A fundamental postulate of criminal jurisprudence is the presumption of innocence, meaning thereby that a person is believed to be innocent until found guilty.

However, there are instances in our criminal law where a reverse onus has been placed on an accused with regard to some specific offences but that is another matter and does not detract from the fundamental postulate in respect of other offences.

Yet another important facet of our criminal jurisprudence is that the grant of bail is the general rule and putting a person in jail or in a prison or in a correction home (whichever expression one may wish to use) is an exception.

Unfortunately,
some of these basic principles appear to have been lost sight of with the result that more and more persons are being incarcerated and for longer periods.
This does not do any good to our criminal jurisprudence or to our society.

3. There is no doubt that the grant or denial of bail is entirely the discretion of the judge considering a case but even so, the exercise of judicial discretion has been circumscribed by a large number of decisions rendered by this Court and by every High Court in the country.
Yet, occasionally there is a necessity to introspect whether denying bail to an accused person is the right thing to do on the facts and in the circumstances of a case.

4. While so introspecting, among the factors that need to be .
considered is whether the accused was arrested during investigations when that person perhaps has the best opportunity to tamper with the evidence or influence _____________________________________________________________________ vs State Of Himachal Pradesh on 13 June, 2024

Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/150708374/
6 witnesses.

If the investigating officer does not find it necessary to arrest an accused person during investigations, a strong case should be made out for placing that person in judicial custody after a charge sheet is filed.

Similarly, it is important to ascertain whether the accused was participating in the investigations to the satisfaction of the investigating officer and was not absconding or not appearing when required by the investigating officer.

Surely, if an accused is not hiding from the investigating officer or is hiding due to some genuine and expressed fear of being victimised, it would be a factor that a judge would need to consider in an appropriate case.

It is also necessary for the judge to consider whether the accused is a first- time offender or has been accused of other offences and if so, the nature of such offences and his or her general conduct.

The poverty or the deemed indigent status of an accused is also an extremely important factor and even Parliament has taken notice of it by incorporating an Explanation to Section 436 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

An equally soft approach to incarceration has been taken by Parliament by inserting Section 436A in the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
5.
To put it shortly, a humane attitude is required to be adopted by a judge, while dealing with an application for remanding a suspect or an accused person to police custody or judicial custody.

There are several reasons for this including maintaining the dignity of an accused person, howsoever poor that person might be, the requirements of Article 21 of the Constitution and the fact that there is enormous overcrowding in prisons, leading to social and other problems as noticed by this Court in In Re-Inhuman Conditions in 1382 Prisons.

entities.text: Prasanta Kumar Sarkar v. Ashis Chatterjee and Another (2010) 14 SCC 496
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text: In view of the aforesaid discussion as well as law laid down by the Hon'ble Apex Court, petitioner has carved out a case for grant of bail, accordingly, the petition is allowed and the petitioner is ordered to be enlarged on bail in aforesaid FIR, subject to his furnishing personal bond in the sum of Rs.2,00,000/- with two local sureties in the like amount to the satisfaction of concerned Chief Judicial Magistrate/trial Court, with following conditions: r (a) He shall make himself available for the purpose of interrogation, if so required and regularly attend the trial Court on each and every date of hearing and if prevented by any reason to do so, seek exemption from appearance by filing appropriate application;
It is clarified that if the petitioner misuses the liberty or violates any of the conditions imposed upon him, the investigating agency shall be free to move this Court for cancellation of the bail.

18. Any observations made hereinabove shall not be construed to be a .
reflection on the merits of the case and shall remain confined to the disposal of this application alone.
The petition stands accordingly disposed of.

19. The bail petitioner is permitted to produce copy of the order downloaded from the High Court Website and the trial court shall not insist for certified copy of the order, however, it may verify the order from the High Court website or otherwise.

ASI Deepak Kumar, PS Sadar, Disrict Mandi, Himachal Pradesh, has also come present with the records.
Records perused and returned.

2. Close scrutiny of record/status report made available to this Court reveals that on 29.5.2024,
victim-prosecutrix (name withheld), aged 36 years, lodged a complaint at Police Station concerned,
alleging therein that she knows the bail petitioner for last four years.
She alleged that .
firstly, the bail petitioner trapped her in his love and thereafter, made her to elope with him.
She alleged that on 20.5.2024, bail petitioner telephonically called her and pressurized her to join his company.
She alleged that since bail petitioner extended threats to commit suicide, she was compelled to join his company.
She alleged that firstly bail petitioner took her to Bilaspur and from there, they both went to Delhi, however, on next day, they again came back to Palampur.
She alleged that since 23.5.2024, they both had been residing in a room taken by the petitioner on rent as husband and wife.
She alleged that during her stay with the petitioner, she was repeatedly sexually assaulted against her wishes by the petitioner and as such, appropriate action in accordance with law be taken.

In the aforesaid background, FIR detailed herein above came to be lodged against the bail petitioner, but before he could be arrested, this Court granted him interim bail vide order dated 12.6.2024, with direction to join the investigation.

Since pursuant to aforesaid order, bail petitioner has joined the investigation and nothing remains to be recovered from him, prayer has been made on his behalf for confirmation of bail granted vide order dated 12.6.2024.
3.

While seriously opposing prayer made by the petitioner, Mr. .
Rajan Kahol, learned Additional Advocate General, submits that though investigation in the case is almost complete, but challan is yet to be filed in the competent court of law and as such, it may not be in the interest of justice to enlarge the bail petitioner on bail.

Mr. Kahol, states that though pursuant to order dated 12.6.2024, petitioner has joined the investigation but keeping in view the gravity of offence alleged to have been committed, he does not deserve any leniency, rather needs to be dealt with in accordance with law.

While making this Court peruse statement of victim- prosecutrix recorded under Section 164 CrPC, Mr. Kahol, states that bail petitioner repeatedly sexually assaulted the victim-prosecutrix against her wishes and as such, no illegality can be said to be committed by the prosecution by registering case under Sections 376 and 506 of IPC.

He states that in the event of petitioner's being enlarged on bail, he may not only flee from justice, but may also cause harm to the victim-prosecutrix and as such, his prayer for grant of bail, may be rejected outrightly.

4 . Having heard learned counsel for the parities and perused material available on record, this court finds that Victim-prosecutrix, aged 36 years, was in contact with the bail petitioner for the last four years.
As per own statements recorded under Section 154 and 164 CrPC, she joined the company of the bail petitioner of her own volition.

Though she .
disclosed to the police as well as Judicial Magistrate that she was compelled to join the company of the bail petitioner w.e.f. 20.5.2024 because the petitioner had threatened to commit suicide, but there is no explanation that why she remained in the company of the bail petitioner w.e.f. 20.5.2024 till 28.5.2024.

As per own statement of the victim- prosecutrix, there had been many occasions, on which, victim-prosecutrix could object or approach the authorities against her illegal confinement as well as forcible sexual assault, if any, yet she failed to do so.

If the statement of victim-prosecutrix, record under Section 164 CrPC is perused in its entirety, it clearly emerges that she and the bail petitioner had been constantly messaging and meeting each other.

On one occasion, message sent by the bail petitioner to the victim-prosecutrix was read by the husband of the victim-prosecutrix and thereafter, some altercation had also taken place inter-se bail petitioner and husband of the victim-prosecutrix.
Though bail petitioner and victim-prosecutrix, both, had agreed to mend their ways, but they kept on meeting each other.

5. Though Mr. Rajan Kahol, learned Additional Advocate General, attempted to argue that bail petitioner repeatedly sexually assaulted the victim-prosecutrix against her wishes, but such plea of him, does not appear to be correct for the reason that victim-prosecutrix, who is major, of .
her own volition, joined the company of the bail petitioner and thereafter, remained in his company for more than a week and during this period, no attempt, if any, was ever made by her to contact her husband or report the matter to the police.

Similarly, this court finds it difficult to agree with Mr.
Rajan Kahol, learned Additional Advocate General that petitioner was unable to understand the consequences of her joining the company of the petitioner, rather conduct of victim-prosecutrix,
which is apparent from the record, suggests something else.

6. Though aforesaid aspects of the matter are to be considered and decided by the court below on the basis of totality of evidence collected on record by the Investigating Agency, but having noticed aforesaid glaring aspects of the matter coupled with the fact that nothing remains to be recovered from the bail petitioner, there appears to be no justification to let the bail petitioner incarcerate in jail for an indefinite period during trial especially when he has made himself available for investigation and nothing remains to be recovered from him.
7. Hon'ble Apex Court as well as this Court in catena of cases have repeatedly held that one is deemed to be innocent till the time, guilt of his/her is not proved in accordance with law.

In the case at hand, guilt if any of the bail petitioner is yet to be established on record by the .

Investigating Agency by leading cogent and convincing evidence and as such, his freedom cannot be curtailed for an indefinite period during trial.

Apprehension expressed by the learned Additional Advocate General that in the event of petitioner's being enlarged on bail, he may flee from justice, can be best met by putting the bail petitioner to stringent conditions as has been fairly stated by the learned counsel for the petitioner.

8. Needless to say, object of the bail is to secure the attendance of the accused in the trial and the proper test to be applied in the solution of the question whether bail should be granted or refused is whether it is probable that the party will appear to take his trial.
Otherwise, bail is not to be withheld as a punishment.
Otherwise also, normal rule is of bail and not jail.
